projects.title: An Exploratory Analysis of Mosaic Chromosomal Aberrations in the Canine Genome: Towards a Comparative Genomics Model
projects.description: Employed Shannon entropy and the MoChA pipeline (from the Broad Institute) to identify 5 novel biomarkers for cancer in canine genomes. First to detect mosaic chromosomal aberrations in dogs; corresponding human biomarkers identified. Findings were presented at the Broad Institute and at the Research Science Institute Symposium. Was identified as a top 300 entry in the Regeneron Science Talent Search.

projects.title: smFRET.ai
projects.description: Designed and deployed a fully functional software suite for data analysis in single molecule FRET experiments with the Kobilka Lab at Stanford School of Medicine. Data filtration process fully automated via an RNN-LSTM pipeline with cross-validation for filtering smFRET time-series trace data.Work integrated into multiple published and internal studies. Examples include:Janetzko, J., Shivnaraine, R., Deutsch, J. C., Shi, Y., Liu, W., Masureel, ... & Kobilka, B. K. (2024). How membranes shape the β-arrestin conformational landscape to provide spatiotemporal control of GPCR desensitization and trafficking. The Journal of Pharmacology and Experimental Therapeutics, 389, 558.Janetzko, J., Inoue, A., Shi, Y., Deutsch, J. C., Ray, K. K., Masureel, M., ... & Shivnaraine, R. (2023). Arrestin C-tail dynamics regulate activation and GPCR engagement. Biophysical Journal, 122(3), 49a.

A lot has happened over the last few months, so thought I’d post an update. In September, Tim Farrelly invited me to Demos Anon, where I showcased a drug discovery tool I’d been working on to predict ADMET properties. While there, I met Lee Sherlock , and a few days before heading back to London I had a great chat with him and Brendan Martin about Meta-flux . Upon returning to London, Joe Michael Sakamura Sissons and I presented our module selection tool as part of the UCL Innovation Lab, where our project was selected for the Student Choice Award! Not long after, I found out that I’d been accepted into the Patch SF fellowship. Spending 10 days in November in the Bay Area was amazing. I visited the Arc Institute and Stanford, met people at EF in San Francisco, and had lunch with Patrick Collison . It really opened my eyes to the range of opportunities and paths available. After more conversations with Lee and Brendan in Dublin, they offered me a part-time role in bioinformatics at Meta-Flux. I'm dropping out of school as an international student in the US to build a startup… Just kidding. I'm legally not allowed to do this. But what I am doing is trying to graduate early so I can jump right back in as soon as possible. That's the thing, we're given opportunities every day, but we have to be able to see them. Opportunities don't wait for you, so you have to fight for them. Back in Februrary, I received a call at 1am to complete a task for a startup. The easy way out was to pretend I was asleep and deal with it the next day, but instead I stayed up until 8am finishing this task despite having an exam later that day. This commitment helped me land a CMO role at this startup, and little did I know, this company would blow up over the summer, giving me the platform I have today. Many of the positive things I'm experiencing in my life now happened because I chased after an opportunity that changed everything. I now have the flexibility to choose what vertical I want to work in and connect with some of the most powerful and interesting people in the space. It was a hard choice to stop applying for internships, put my full trust in something not as stable as a corporate job, and work long hours throughout the summer, but now I'm living a much more comfortable life. Not in the physical sense, as I plan on flying between school and SF to continue working on my current startup, but in the way where I can put the puzzle pieces of my life together faster to reach my dreams. I used to be scared of saying yes from a fear of failure, but now I take in whatever opportunities come my way. I put myself in places that spark conversations or introductions, and no longer fear "looking stupid" for asking questions that may guide me in the right direction. As recruiting season fires up again, just remember to stay proactive. Go for every opportunity you see, no matter how far-fetched it may seem. I just landed at the new La Guardia terminal and the first thing I see is this dog shit software from the 90s This place is one of the most futuristic airports in the country - costing 8 billion dollars - yet this is the state of the software. The reason? An enterprise doesn’t buy software because of what it can do. They never have. And they never will. They buy software because of how easy it is to install. Does it come with an army of consultants to implement? Does it comply with the regulations of my industry? Is the sales rep buddies with the contractor I work with and has my entire process mapped out before I pick up the phone? That is why shitty software wins. Stop innovating on the wrong things. ...more ...more
